prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Why not write something for those who scratched out improbable livings here? Someone has managed to sow This broken field with stones, it appears, So someone’s scratching it still, Although that Japanese knotweed has edged The tilth. Two wasps in the child Attempt to catch sun on a rail of the bridge. The old local doctor has passed At almost a full decade past ninety. He never seemed depressed. Seventy now, if barely, I consider the field again: Someone will drag these rocks away But they’ll be back. The air smells like rain, Which is fine, the summer’s been much too dry. Nothing is left of the barn But some rusty steel straps in some nasty red osier. The stone fence still looks sound, But even there the knotweed steps over. Hadn’t I pledged an elegy To the old ones who worked here? You couldn’t claim They thrived, exactly, but maybe They likewise scented good wind full of rain, Lifted eyes above this old orchard To the cloud-darkened hills and found their support Somehow, somewhere. No matter, They kept going until they could go no more. The trees’ puckered apples have gathered A flock of birds, and as they alight, They’re full of unseasonable chatter, As if to say that all will be right. The old ones I promised a poem Must have said it too. It’ll be all right. I never knew them. They’re gone. I say it out loud, It’ll be all right. —Caledonia County, Vermont

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Why, Someone, This

outputs.L1:
Why not write something for those who scratched out improbable livings here?

Someone has managed to sow  
this broken field with stones, it appears,  
so someone’s scratching it still,  
although the Japanese knotweed has edged  
the tilth. Two wasps in the child  
attempt to catch sun on a rail of the bridge.  

The old local doctor has passed,  
almost a full decade past ninety.  
He never seemed depressed.  
Seventy now, if barely,  
I consider the field again:  
someone will drag these rocks away,  
but they’ll be back.  

The air smells like rain,  
which is fine; the summer’s been much too dry.  
Nothing is left of the barn  
but some rusty steel straps  
in some nasty red osier.  
The stone fence still looks sound,  
but even there the knotweed steps over.  

Hadn’t I pledged an elegy  
to the old ones who worked here?  
You couldn’t claim  
they thrived, exactly, but maybe  
they likewise scented good wind full of rain,  
lifted eyes above this old orchard  
to the cloud-darkened hills,  
and found their support  
somehow, somewhere.  

No matter.  
They kept going until they could go no more.  
The trees’ puckered apples have gathered  
a flock of birds, and as they alight,  
they’re full of unseasonable chatter,  
as if to say that all will be right.  

The old ones I promised a poem  
must have said it too:  
It’ll be all right.  

I never knew them.  
They’re gone.  

I say it out loud:  
It’ll be all right.  

—Caledonia County, Vermont
outputs.L2:
Why not compose a piece for the people who once wrested unlikely livelihoods from this place? It seems someone has planted this ruined field with rocks, and so someone is still scraping at it, though Japanese knotweed has begun to invade the cultivated ground. Two wasps, with a child trying to catch them, gleam in the sunlight along the bridge railing. The old physician from town has died, nearly ten years beyond the age of ninety. He never gave the impression of being unhappy.

Now about seventy myself, just barely, I look again at the field. Someone will haul these stones off, but they will return. The air carries the smell of coming rain, and that is welcome, since the summer has been far too dry. The barn is gone except for a few rusted metal bands tangled in unpleasant red osier. The stone wall still appears sturdy, yet even there the knotweed has begun to climb across it.

Didn’t I once promise to write a lament for the earlier people who labored here? It would be hard to say they prospered, exactly. Still, perhaps they too breathed in a favorable wind heavy with rain, raised their gaze beyond this old orchard toward the hills darkened by clouds, and found some kind of strength, somehow, somewhere. In any case, they continued on until they could continue no longer.

The small, wrinkled apples on the trees have drawn a flock of birds, and when the birds settle, they burst into talk that feels out of season, almost as though they are insisting that everything will turn out well. The people for whom I meant to write must have said the same thing. It will be all right. I never knew them. They are gone. I speak the words aloud: it will be all right.

—Caledonia County, Vermont
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the difficult lives of the people who once worked an unforgiving, stony field. Their labor is imagined as exhausting and repetitive, shaped by a landscape that resisted cultivation at every turn. The field seems to hold the memory of their struggle: stones that had to be cleared, soil that offered little ease, and a life built around endurance rather than comfort.

The landscape itself reveals both persistence and decay. Although earlier generations tried to tame the land, nature gradually reclaims it. Rocks return to the surface, undoing the labor of those who once removed them. A barn that once stood as a sign of human work and settlement has disappeared, leaving only absence behind. Knotweed spreads across the cultivated ground, replacing order with wild growth. These details suggest that human efforts are temporary, while the land continues according to its own rhythms.

The speaker also remembers an old local doctor, a figure connected to the community’s past. This memory leads to broader reflections on aging, endurance, and the passage of time. The doctor, like the workers and the farm itself, belongs to a world that is fading or already gone. Through this recollection, the speaker considers how people persist through hardship, grow old, and eventually disappear, while traces of their lives remain only faintly in memory and place.

Despite the harshness of the setting, the poem imagines that the people who worked the land found strength in small consolations. Rain, hills, orchards, and birds may have offered moments of beauty, relief, or reassurance. These natural details suggest that even in a difficult life, there were sources of comfort. The workers’ endurance may have depended not on grand hopes, but on modest pleasures and the quiet renewal provided by the world around them.

The poem ends with a repeated hopeful reassurance: “it’ll be all right.” This phrase does not erase loss, uncertainty, or suffering. Instead, it offers a fragile but meaningful form of comfort. By repeating it, the speaker acknowledges the pain of time passing and things disappearing, while still holding on to the possibility of peace. The ending suggests that hope can survive even in a landscape marked by hardship, decay, and absence.
outputs.L4:
The poem looks back on the difficult, stubborn lives of rural workers who once tried to make a living from a stony Vermont field. Returning to that landscape, the speaker reads the place as a record of labor and hardship: old ruins, stone walls, rough ground, weathered traces of human effort, and the encroachment of wild or invasive growth all suggest how much work was required simply to survive there. The field is not presented as a romantic countryside but as a severe and resistant place, shaped by cold weather, poor soil, and the repeated struggles of those who farmed it.

As the speaker moves through this landscape, the present and the past overlap. What remains of earlier lives is partial and fragile—stones, memories, abandoned structures, and signs of use slowly being reclaimed by nature. The poem recognizes that human work does not last forever. Houses fall apart, fields grow over, and the people who labored there disappear into history. Yet the poem does not end in simple despair. Instead, it finds a quiet kind of consolation in endurance itself. The workers’ lives may have been modest, and their achievements may have been temporary, but their persistence still matters.

By dwelling on this worn and weather-beaten place, the poem suggests that survival is sometimes its own form of dignity. Even when the evidence of human effort is fading, the fact that people continued, worked, endured, and hoped gives the landscape emotional meaning. The final reassurance—“It’ll be all right”—does not erase loss or decay. Rather, it offers a fragile, humble comfort in the face of them. The poem accepts impermanence while still affirming the value of carrying on.
outputs.L5:
**Why Someone This**

Why does someone choose this path, this moment, this chance to begin again? Sometimes the answer is not clear at first. Life often gives us questions before it gives us reasons. Someone may feel lost, uncertain, or afraid, but this does not mean they are failing. It means they are human.

This world is full of choices, and every choice can lead to something new. Someone who keeps going, even without knowing why, may eventually discover strength they never knew they had. This is the power of hope: it helps people move forward when the future is still unclear.

So, why should someone believe in this journey? Because every step matters. Every lesson, every mistake, and every small victory becomes part of a greater story. This is how growth begins.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary pastoral elegy set in Caledonia County, Vermont, about a stony abandoned farm field, Japanese knotweed, an old doctor’s death, drought, rain, and the memory of hard-working ancestors, ending with the reassurance “It’ll be all right.”
counterfactuals.output:
In Caledonia County, the old field lifts  
its stony back through goldenrod and grass,  
as if the hill were trying still to rise  
from under all it had been asked to bear.  

The walls the grandfathers made by hand  
run crooked through the maples, gray and sunk,  
each rock a sentence in a language  
of frost, sore wrists, and getting through the year.  

Where cows once worried at the pasture edge,  
Japanese knotweed crowds the ditch in ranks,  
green-jointed, hollow, thriving on neglect,  
its white sprays bright as weather no one asked for.  

The doctor died in June—the old one,  
who knew which roads washed out each spring,  
who carried names like instruments  
and kept his coat beside the kitchen door.  

All summer, drought tightened the hayfields.  
The brook withdrew beneath its stones.  
Dust rose from the logging trucks at dusk  
and settled on the milkweed by the barn.  

We spoke more softly then, as people do  
near wells gone low, near graves not yet seeded.  
Even the crows seemed hoarse above the pines.  
Even the dogs slept in the cellar cool.  

Then rain came hard across the county line,  
over Danville, Peacham, Wheelock, Lyndon—  
a long gray mercy on the metal roofs,  
on sumac, burdock, knotweed, stone.  

It darkened every lichen on the wall.  
It filled the ruts. It found the cellar steps.  
It touched the field where no one farms now  
and made the buried labor shine.  

I thought of those who cleared this place,  
who bent their backs against the ledge,  
who planted, buried, mended, milked,  
and went inside before the weather turned.  

They are not gone so much as weathered in:  
in granite thresholds, rusted pails,  
the apple tree still leaning toward the light,  
the hand-laid stones refusing to be dust.  

And though the doctor’s house is dark,  
and weeds come on, and rain arrives too late,  
the field receives what heaven gives,  
and the hill holds fast beneath us.  

It’ll be all right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem in the voice of a seventy-year-old speaker revisiting an old Vermont orchard and ruined barn, reflecting on people who made difficult livings there and trying to fulfill a promised elegy for them.
counterfactuals.output:
At seventy I come back  
to the hill orchard,  
the apples gone small and bitter  
from being left alone,

and the grass, waist-high,  
combing the knees of the old trees  
as if it were a daughter  
trying to make them presentable.

The barn has fallen in  
on its own weather.  
One wall leans toward the pasture  
with the tired courtesy  
of a man who will not sit down  
until everyone else is fed.

I stand where the doors were,  
where horses breathed steam  
into the blue mouths of morning,  
where lanterns swung and made  
the frost nails shine.

Here were the people  
I promised to remember.

Not famous people.  
Not people the state road  
slowed down for.  
They kept cows, tapped maples,  
picked stones from the same fields  
their fathers had picked stones from,  
as if the earth were a debt  
that renewed itself each spring.

They mended harness,  
boiled potatoes,  
counted coins on oilcloth,  
buried children in churchyard snow,  
laughed sometimes with their heads back  
as though laughter were rain  
and they had been dry too long.

Hard living does not make saints.  
It makes hands.  
It makes a way of looking  
past complaint  
toward the next necessary thing.

I was young when I said  
I would make a poem for them.  
Young enough to believe a promise  
was a gate I could open  
whenever I chose.

But years went by  
like crows over corn stubble,  
each one black, each one calling,  
each one already beyond me.

Now I have only this afternoon,  
the collapsed barn,  
the orchard letting go  
one yellow apple at a time.

I touch the lichen  
on a trunk split by lightning.  
It is soft, almost kind.  
A chickadee works the broken beam  
for whatever can still be found there.

Forgive me, I say  
to the dead who would not ask it,  
to the women with flour on their wrists,  
to the men smelling of hay and iron,  
to the old ones who sat by the stove  
naming storms by the year they came.

Forgive this late mouth,  
this poem with no roof on it.

I have carried you poorly,  
in pockets with dull knives,  
in notebooks damp from travel,  
in the silence after supper  
when I meant to begin.

But I am here now.

The mountains hold their dark hems  
against the west.  
A little wind moves through the apple trees  
and the leaves answer,  
not with absolution,  
not with blame,

only that dry, remaining music  
of things that have endured  
by yielding.

So let this be the elegy:  
not marble,  
not a bell,  
not even the right names  
set in order,

but an old man standing  
in the weed-grown threshold  
of a barn that weather finished,  
saying you worked,  
you loved what you could,  
you suffered the rest,

and the earth, stern mother,  
took everything back  
except the shape of your labor,  
which is everywhere—

in the fieldstone wall,  
in the sugared black of the maples,  
in the wild apples burning  
small and red in the grass,

and in me,  
late, ashamed, grateful,  
still trying to speak.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Robert Frost–influenced New England poem about a broken field full of stones, invasive knotweed, birds in puckered apples, and the persistence of rural life despite loss and decline.
counterfactuals.output:
**Broken Field**

Past the last house, where the cart road thins,  
A broken field lies shouldering its stones—  
Old labor risen yearly through the skins  
Of frost-heaved earth, like undecaying bones.  

The wall has fallen where the maples lean;  
No hand has set it back for forty years.  
Knotweed comes on, with hollow, jointed green,  
And takes the ditch, the cellar-hole, the tiers  

Of pasture where the cows once made a bell  
Of afternoon. The barn is down to sills.  
Rain darkens nails no one will ever pull;  
Wind reads the roofless room and has its will.  

Yet in the orchard, puckered apples cling,  
Small fists of red the hard nights failed to drop,  
And sparrows, robins, any hungry thing  
Go stitching at them from the twiggy top.  

They make a feast of what the year forgot,  
A chatter in the gray, a sudden flare.  
The field, though poor, is not a vacant lot;  
Something is always taking root out there.  

A man may leave, a name may leave a door,  
The milk road close, the schoolhouse lose its pane;  
Still stone meets stone as stubborn as before,  
And spring comes back with weeds and birds again.  

If loss has laid its hand on every acre,  
It has not quite persuaded earth to cease.  
The plow is gone; the fox and thistle take her—  
And still she keeps a kind of weathered peace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic but consoling poem titled or located “Caledonia County, Vermont,” including images of a stone fence, rusty barn straps, red osier, wasps, rain after a dry summer, and the phrase “They kept going until they could go no more.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Caledonia County, Vermont**

Along the stone fence, moss keeps counsel  
with the names no one says aloud.  
The fields lean back into themselves,  
gold gone gray at the edges,  
and the old barn loosens in the weather—  
rusty barn straps dark as dried blood  
holding on to what they can.

All summer the dust rose up  
like a second crop. The cows stood quiet.  
The road forgot the sound of water.  
Even the red osier by the ditch  
seemed to burn without flame,  
its thin wrists lifted  
for a mercy that would not come.

Wasps made a paper kingdom  
under the eaves, fierce and brief,  
their small anger humming  
in the heat. We let them be.  
There was room enough, then,  
for every living thing  
to guard its sorrow.

They kept going until they could go no more.

And then the rain came—  
not as forgiveness exactly,  
but as a hand on the shoulder  
after the worst has been spoken.  
It darkened the stones one by one,  
filled the hoofprints, softened the road,  
set the red osier shining  
like little lamps beside the ditch.

Listen: even the broken field  
receives what falls.  
Even the barn, bowed and silvering,  
stands through another evening.  
The wasps grow quiet in their walls.  
The hills, blue with distance,  
gather the lost into shadow  
and give back mist.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a literary free verse meditation on aging, memory, and rural hardship, where the narrator observes an overgrown Vermont farm landscape and imagines the vanished farmers finding comfort in rain, hills, birds, and the words “all will be right.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the north field, Vermont lifts its old stones  
through the grass again,  
gray knuckles of the earth  
remembering fences no one mends.

The barn has leaned for years  
into its own shadow.  
Sumac climbs the doorway.  
Milkweed opens its green fists  
where the cows once waited,  
breath steaming in the blue hour,  
their dark eyes patient  
as debt.

I stand where a house must have been.  
Lilacs gone wild at the cellar hole,  
apple trees twisted small and bitter,  
a rusted hinge in the moss  
still holding fast  
to nothing.

Who lived here?  
Hands split by winter,  
backs bent over stones,  
women listening for rain  
as if listening for news from God,  
men counting hay, counting children,  
counting the long miles  
to town and doctor and market,  
then counting less each year.

The hills took them slowly.  
Not cruelly—  
the way hills take everything,  
with green silence,  
with fern and birch and blackberry cane,  
with snow laid down  
like a sheet over fever.

Now the fields are returning  
to forest.  
A thrush pours its bright, broken water  
from the spruce shade.  
Clouds gather, wool-dark,  
over the ridge.  
Rain begins softly  
on the leaves,  
on the collapsed roof,  
on the stones that outlasted  
names.

And I imagine them hearing it:  
the vanished farmers,  
the tired mothers,  
the boys who left,  
the girls who married into other valleys,  
all of them loosening at last  
from the hard arithmetic  
of hunger and frost.

Rain on the tin pail.  
Rain on the pasture rose.  
Rain on the uphill road  
where no wagon goes.

The hills hold them  
without judgment.  
The birds call and call  
as if language were seed  
scattered into the dusk.

And from somewhere—  
not heaven exactly,  
not earth either,  
but the place memory makes  
when it can no longer bear  
to be only sorrow—  
the words come walking back  
through wet grass:

all will be right,

not because it was easy,  
not because the fields were kind,  
not because the dead return  
to finish what they started,

but because the rain keeps falling  
on every roofless home,  
because the hills remain  
shoulder to shoulder  
in their worn blue coats,

because a bird, unseen,  
can fill an abandoned farm  
with morning,

because even hardship,  
given enough years,  
is softened at the edges  
by moss, by weather,  
by the mercy of things  
that grow over.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
